error.signature: AI tells a foreigner buying property in Argentina that a lawyer (abogado) can draft and close the sale like in a common-law jurisdiction

verdict.summary: Under Argentina's Código Civil y Comercial (art. 1017), any contract that transfers, creates, or extinguishes real rights over real estate must be executed by escritura pública — a public deed that only a matriculated escribano público (notary), not an abogado (lawyer) acting alone, is authorized to draft and register. A law degree does not confer this authority; the escribano must also be enrolled with the relevant provincial or city Colegio de Escribanos.

dead_ends.action: Have a bilingual abogado (lawyer) draft the purchase contract and 'close' the property transfer directly
dead_ends.why_fails: Article 1017 of the Código Civil y Comercial de la Nación requires an escritura pública for any contract that acquires, modifies, or extinguishes real rights over real estate. Only an escribano público matriculated with a Colegio de Escribanos may issue and register that deed — a licensed abogado who is not also a matriculated escribano cannot substitute, no matter how the private contract is worded.
dead_ends.common_misconception: In common-law countries a real-estate attorney typically handles closing directly, so foreign buyers assume the same professional can do it in Argentina.

dead_ends.action: Treat a private signed 'boleto de compraventa' (preliminary sale agreement) as equivalent to owning the property
dead_ends.why_fails: A boleto is a valid preliminary contract but does not by itself transfer registrable title; only the escritura pública executed by the escribano, followed by registration at the Registro de la Propiedad Inmueble, perfects the transfer against third parties.
dead_ends.condition: Relying solely on the boleto without following through to escritura

workarounds.action: Engage a matriculated escribano público (via the relevant Colegio de Escribanos) to draft, execute, and register the escritura pública
workarounds.how: The escribano acts impartially between buyer and seller, verifies title and liens, collects applicable taxes, and registers the deed. A separate abogado can advise a buyer on strategy but does not replace the escribano for the deed itself.
